The ACS 1-year share moves +0.56 points in 2007 (fell in 38% of counties) and +0.21 points in 2009 (fell in 43% of counties); the mean absolute ACS year-to-year move in the other years is 0.31 points, which is the sampling-noise scale of 1-year county estimates. The ACS shows no 2007 step comparable to LODES. The ACS shows no 2009 step comparable to LODES. See the pooled rows above for the aggregate picture.

Note the 2010->2011 LODES jump in Cole (+6.4 pts), Greene (+4.5 pts), Jasper (+8.8 pts) (ACS 2011 change in the same counties: +0.1, -0.6, +3.2 pts): a LODES-side discontinuity with no counterpart in the ACS (possibly the 2010-11 entry of federal workers and/or a change in Missouri employer address assignment; not investigated here).

Summary: slopes 2009-2019, mean across counties ACS -0.096 pts/yr vs LODES -0.402 pts/yr (worker-weighted -0.006 vs -0.330); cross-county correlation of slopes r = 0.45 (n = 51); counties where both slopes have the same sign: 31/51. 2019->2023 change: mean ACS +2.39 pts vs LODES -1.40 pts, r = 0.27.

Interpretation: over 2009-2019 the ACS 5-year share is nearly flat (worker-weighted -0.01 pts/yr) while the LODES window mean falls -0.33 pts/yr; the cross-county ordering agrees moderately (r = 0.45) but the LODES decline is broader (negative LODES slope in 48/51 counties vs ACS 30/51). The 2019->2023 divergence runs the other way: the ACS share rises in 35/51 counties (mean +2.39 pts; Illinois counties +5.68, Missouri +2.14) because B08007 assigns people who work from home to their county of residence, so the post-2020 remote-work shift raises the ACS in-county share mechanically, whereas LODES keeps assigning those jobs to the employer's establishment address and its window mean keeps drifting down.

Figure: `outputs/external/figures/acs5_vs_lodes_slopes.png`.

## (iii) Caveats

- ACS estimates carry sampling error. 1-year county estimates (65,000+ population) have margins of error on the in-county share of roughly 1-3 points for the large counties and more for the smaller ones; year-to-year moves of that size are noise, so only a step that is both large and common to most counties is evidence. MOEs were not extracted here (the m-files are in the same zips if needed).
- 5-year releases overlap: consecutive windows share four of five sample years, so the 11 'slopes' over 2009-2019 are fitted to heavily autocorrelated points and the effective number of independent windows is about 2-3. The LODES comparison series is averaged over the identical calendar windows, so this affects both series equally but inflates the apparent smoothness of both.
- The ACS universe is workers 16+ who worked last week (residence-based, place of work as reported, including self-employed and workers not covered by UI); LODES covers UI-covered jobs (plus federal from 2010) with workplace and residence as recorded administratively, and includes multiple jobholding. Levels are therefore not expected to agree; the comparison is about changes.
- 2020 has no standard ACS 1-year release; the 2016-20 5-year release is included (sequence-based files) but its 2020 sample is affected by the pandemic non-response and the Bureau's experimental weighting.
- Pre-2010 1-year counties: only counties with population 65,000+ are published (16 in Missouri, 4-5 in Kansas and Illinois within the metros), so the 2005-2009 comparison covers the core counties only. Smaller metro counties enter only through the 5-year series (first release 2005-09).
- County of residence vs county of work in ACS is self-reported place of work (address of the workplace last week); for people with no fixed workplace it is where they reported to, which can differ from the LODES administrative workplace (often an employer's reporting unit).
- LODES state coverage: the 'all 51 counties' LODES share uses MO, KS and IL OD files plus the out-of-state residence file where available; cross-state flows for counties on the state line (Kansas City, St. Louis) depend on the partner state's file being present for that year.
